Git Internals for Software Forensics

You already use Git every day. This primer explains the few ideas underneath it: enough to see why two matching hashes can settle a question about thousands of files, and where a hash stops being evidence.

Every hash and every piece of command output below comes from a small demo repository that a script builds from scratch, so you can rebuild it and follow along. Reading time is about 20 minutes. A cheat sheet is at the end.

Also available: this primer as a PDF, and the one-page cheat sheet (PDF).

1 Git is a content-addressed database

Most of us picture Git as a chain of diffs. It isn’t one. Underneath, Git is a key-value store: you give it some bytes, it stores them, and it hands back a key. The key is the hash of the bytes. Branches, history, diffs and renames are all built on top of that one idea.

Two things follow. The same content always gets the same key, on any machine, in any repository. And content cannot change without its key changing, so a key names exactly one piece of content.

The hash is SHA-1, written as 40 hex characters and usually shortened to the first seven or so. Git uses a hardened SHA-1 that detects the known collision attacks, and newer repositories can use SHA-256 instead (64 characters, same ideas).

$ git hash-object src/util.py
4af79c158719bdf44e8c6296c08019724f549d69
$ (printf 'blob %d\0' "$(wc -c < src/util.py)"; cat src/util.py) | sha1sum
4af79c158719bdf44e8c6296c08019724f549d69  -

git hash-object works on any file, inside a repository or not. The second command shows there is no magic in it: a file’s key is the SHA-1 of a short header (the word blob, the size in bytes, a zero byte) followed by the file’s contents.

Why this matters forensically

A Git hash is a fingerprint you can compute yourself from the material in front of you. You do not have to trust the repository, the tool, or whoever handed it over. If the bytes hash to the value, they are the bytes.

2 The four object types

Everything Git stores is one of four kinds of object. Figure 1 shows one of each from the demo repository.

A blob is the contents of a file and nothing else. It has no filename, no path, no permissions and no timestamp. git cat-file shows any object’s type (-t), size (-s) and content (-p):

$ git cat-file -t 4af79c1
blob
$ git cat-file -s 4af79c1
54
$ git cat-file -p 4af79c1
def total(amounts):
    return round(sum(amounts), 2)

A tree is a directory: a sorted list of entries, each holding a mode, a name, and the hash of a blob (a file) or of another tree (a subdirectory). Names and permissions live here. The modes you will meet are 100644 (file), 100755 (executable file), 120000 (symlink), 040000 (subdirectory) and 160000 (submodule).

$ git cat-file -p 85f2af6
100644 blob 6903f7a3b2fdc1144034a5cc082224dfef4eb6d4  README.md
040000 tree 964f13d0f07fae6ae3c604c03db02f31d551b4a3  docs
040000 tree 52dc7bb71bff532f297dd440194ab13f2bc55c58  src

Because a blob is only bytes, two files with the same content are one blob, however many places they appear. Renaming a file or making it executable creates no new blob either. Only the tree changes:

$ git ls-tree -r ec7b6b5
100644 blob 6903f7a3b2fdc1144034a5cc082224dfef4eb6d4  README.md
100644 blob 1d1849599c93a66f5cab62cdc0232f8214f1f939  docs/handbook.md
100644 blob b6d66e86ef07a36afd15c9bb0e0796af6efe4690  src/main.py
100644 blob 4af79c158719bdf44e8c6296c08019724f549d69  src/util.py
100644 blob 53d199d479a01023ca6f7e09c004fc9f681a17d6  tools/run.sh
100644 blob 4af79c158719bdf44e8c6296c08019724f549d69  tools/util.py
$ git ls-tree 253a528 tools/
100755 blob 53d199d479a01023ca6f7e09c004fc9f681a17d6  tools/run.sh
100644 blob 4af79c158719bdf44e8c6296c08019724f549d69  tools/util.py

src/util.py and tools/util.py are one blob listed twice. After chmod +x, run.sh keeps its blob hash and only its mode differs. (Two details for anyone recomputing tree hashes by hand: Git cannot store an empty directory, and entries are sorted as if directory names ended in /.)

A commit is a short piece of text. It holds the hash of one root tree, the hashes of its parent commits (none for the first commit, usually two for a merge), an author line and a committer line, each with a Unix time and a timezone offset, an optional signature, and the message.

$ git cat-file -p 06ade68
tree 85f2af666745dfc198f7a5c0f671be0ee64007e8
parent 727ea5ce7707e09face7bfca4fb2f949dc50edb8
author Ada Example <ada@example.com> 1709562600 +0000
committer Ada Example <ada@example.com> 1709562600 +0000

Fix rounding in util.py

An annotated tag is a named pointer to another object, usually a commit, with its own tagger, date, message and optional signature. Branches and lightweight tags are not objects at all. Each is just a name for one hash.

Why this matters forensically

Know which object answers which question. “Is this the same file?” is a blob question. “Is this the same directory, with the same names and permissions?” is a tree question. “Is this the same project state with the same history?” is a commit question.

3 Snapshots, not diffs

A commit does not store what changed. It points to one root tree, and that tree is a complete snapshot of every file in the project at that moment.

That sounds wasteful, but nothing is copied. A commit that changes one file gets a new blob for that file and new trees for the directories above it. Everything else is referred to by the same hashes as before. In the demo, the second commit edits only src/util.py:

$ git rev-parse 727ea5c:docs 06ade68:docs
964f13d0f07fae6ae3c604c03db02f31d551b4a3
964f13d0f07fae6ae3c604c03db02f31d551b4a3
$ git rev-parse 727ea5c:src 06ade68:src
3055bb645492e112d43a09a17963ddd2fde411c6
52dc7bb71bff532f297dd440194ab13f2bc55c58

docs has the same tree hash in both commits, so it is the same stored object. src has a new one.

The diffs you see in git log -p or in a pull request are computed on demand by comparing two snapshots. They are a view of the record, not the record.

Why this matters forensically

Any commit can be examined on its own as a complete copy of the code at that point. When someone describes “the changes in a commit”, they are describing a comparison that Git computed. The snapshots on either side are the evidence.

4 The Merkle structure

Put the last two sections together. A tree’s hash is computed from its entries, and each entry contains the hash of a child. So a tree’s hash depends on everything underneath it. This arrangement is called a Merkle tree.

Change one byte in one file and its blob hash changes. That changes the entry in its directory’s tree, so that tree’s hash changes, and so on up to the root tree and the commit. Nothing else moves. Sibling files and directories keep their hashes.

The same thing happens along history. Each commit contains its parents’ hashes, so a commit’s hash depends on its entire ancestry. Merges have two parents, which makes history a graph and not a line (a Merkle DAG).

$ git log --graph --oneline
* a30b4b9 Release 1.0
*   410cc9f Merge branch 'feature'
|\
| * 3d516dd Add --verbose flag
* | 909aece Add currency setting
|/
* 253a528 Make run.sh executable
* ec7b6b5 Add tools directory
* 7058063 Rename guide to handbook
* 06ade68 Fix rounding in util.py
* 727ea5c Initial project

Three consequences do most of the work in forensic analysis:

  1. Equal tree hashes mean identical directories: every name, every mode and every byte, all the way down. There is nothing further to inspect.
  2. Equal commit hashes mean identical content and identical history, back to the first commit.
  3. Any change changes every hash above it: the trees up to the root, that commit, and every commit descended from it.

Why this matters forensically

One 40-character comparison can stand in for comparing thousands of files. If two repositories agree on a tree hash, you can state that those directories are byte-for-byte identical without opening a file, and anyone can check the claim independently.

5 What a hash proves, and what it doesn’t

A hash proves identity of content. For a commit, that content includes the exact ancestry. That is all it proves.

It does not prove when something happened or who did it. The author and committer names, emails and dates in a commit are plain text supplied by whoever created it, and Git records whatever it is given. Every name and date in this primer’s demo repository was set by a script, and every hash in it is perfectly valid. A rewritten history is just as internally consistent as an original one.

Two things can anchor a commit to the outside world:

  • A signature. Commits and tags can be signed with a GPG or SSH key. Commits created through GitHub’s web interface, such as merges made with the merge button, are typically signed by GitHub’s own “web-flow” key, which shows that GitHub created that commit object.
  • An independent record of the hash. If a commit hash appears in an email, a produced document, a CI log or a public copy with a known date, then that commit and everything it depends on existed by then.

A signature is computed over the commit’s content, and that content includes the tree hash and the parent hashes. So a valid signature on one commit vouches for its whole snapshot and for every commit reachable from it.

$ git verify-commit a30b4b9
gpg: Signature made Fri Mar 15 10:00:00 2024 UTC
gpg:                using EDDSA key D35B7073DE677DC3BA4DC7867E5FDA60395E9A41
gpg: Good signature from "Ada Example <ada@example.com>" [unknown]
gpg: WARNING: This key is not certified with a trusted signature!
gpg:          There is no indication that the signature belongs to the owner.
Primary key fingerprint: D35B 7073 DE67 7DC3 BA4D  C786 7E5F DA60 395E 9A41

Read that output carefully. “Good signature” means this key signed exactly this commit. The warning underneath is GPG saying it has no basis for connecting the key to a person. That link has to come from somewhere else, such as a key published on the person’s account. The signature’s own date also comes from the signer’s clock.

One caution: verifying a signature runs external programs named in Git’s configuration, and a repository’s own .git/config can point gpg.program at anything. Inspect the configuration of an untrusted repository before running commands inside it (section 14).

Why this matters forensically

Be precise about which claim you are making. “These files are identical to those” is a hash claim and is as strong as the hash function. “This was written on 4 March by Ada” is a metadata claim and needs corroboration from signatures or outside records.

6 Rewritten history

A commit’s hash covers its content, its parents and its metadata, so history can never be edited in place. The tools that appear to edit it (commit --amend, rebase, cherry-pick, squash merges, filter-repo, filter-branch) build new commits and move the branch to them. The result is a new, valid history with different hashes.

To show the effect, the demo repository was cloned and run through git filter-repo --path src/, which rebuilds history as if only the src directory had ever existed. A producing party might do the same to limit a production to the directories in scope.

The table below pairs the commits of the two repositories by message, author and date, then prints the commit hashes and the src tree hash on each side:

$ ../pair-commits.sh original filtered src
subject                   original  filtered   original:src  filtered:src
Initial project           727ea5c   4391306    3055bb6       3055bb6       same
Fix rounding in util.py   06ade68   9718e64    52dc7bb       52dc7bb       same
Rename guide to handbook  7058063   -          52dc7bb       -
Add tools directory       ec7b6b5   -          52dc7bb       -
Make run.sh executable    253a528   -          52dc7bb       -
Add currency setting      909aece   69b0a9e    01474df       01474df       same
Add --verbose flag        3d516dd   6a06b56    51e6743       51e6743       same
Merge branch 'feature'    410cc9f   bbb113c    f761857       f761857       same
Release 1.0               a30b4b9   a8b1208    003e373       003e373       same

Every surviving commit has a new hash. Three commits have no counterpart because they touched only docs or tools. The signature on the release commit is gone, because the commit it signed no longer exists in this history. But the src tree hash at each surviving commit is unchanged, because a tree hash depends only on what is under it.

Fingerprints of rewriting:

  • the same messages, authors and dates under different commit hashes;
  • identical trees under different commit hashes (only metadata, parents or a signature changed);
  • commits in one copy with no counterpart in the other;
  • signatures that are missing or fail where the other copy’s verify;
  • more than one root commit (git rev-list --max-parents=0 --all), or committer dates bunched at the time of the rewrite.

The pairing technique generalizes. Compare each pair at three levels: commit hash, then root tree hash, then subtree hashes. That tells you exactly what differs and where. When two copies share the start of a long history, you can binary-search git rev-list --first-parent --reverse for the first commit hash that differs, because once commit hashes diverge they never agree again.

Why this matters forensically

Different commit hashes do not mean different code, and a rewritten history is not in itself a sign of bad faith. Filtering a production is routine. What matters is being able to show precisely what was kept, what was changed and what was dropped.

7 Comparing two repositories

The usual task: one repository produced in a case, and a second copy from somewhere else, such as an earlier production, an open-source upstream or a copy obtained through another channel. Work from the cheapest check to the most detailed.

  1. Look for shared commit hashes. Run git rev-list --all in each and compare the lists. One shared commit means everything up to that commit is identical in both.
  2. Compare tree hashes for the directories you care about. git rev-parse <commit>:<path> prints the hash of the directory at that path in that commit.
  3. Descend only where hashes differ. git ls-tree <commit> <path> lists one level, and git ls-tree -r lists every file with its blob hash. With both histories fetched into one scratch repository, git diff --stat <a> <b> does the descent for you.
$ git -C original rev-parse v1.0:src
003e373c17b454025f98e13148cb935808e471e5
$ git -C filtered rev-parse v1.0:src
003e373c17b454025f98e13148cb935808e471e5
$ git -C compare diff --stat v1.0 filtered/main
 README.md        | 5 -----
 docs/handbook.md | 5 -----
 tools/run.sh     | 2 --
 tools/util.py    | 2 --
 4 files changed, 14 deletions(-)

The two src directories are identical. The complete snapshots differ only by the files the filter removed.

Keep one limit in mind. A matching tree hash verifies that snapshot. It says nothing about how the directory got there, and the two histories behind it may differ. To verify history, pair the commits and compare at each pair, as in section 6.

Why this matters forensically

This is how you establish that material from an uncontrolled source is the same as what was produced, or show exactly where it is not, without reading either one line by line.

8 Case study: a production and an unofficial copy

This is an anonymized account of a real pattern.

A party produced a source repository for inspection in a secure review room. Separately, the attorneys received an unofficial copy of the source code through a channel other than the producing party. It was said to be authentic, and more complete than the production made on the record. If it matched the production, the analysis could be done on the unofficial copy with ordinary tools, outside the review room.

They did not obviously match. The production held only some of the top-level directories, and the unofficial copy held many more. No commit hash appeared in both. That is what section 6 predicts: the production had been rebuilt to contain only those directories, so every one of its commits was new.

So the analyst compared tree hashes instead: git rev-parse HEAD:<directory> for each produced directory in the review room, and the same command on the unofficial copy. Every one matched.

That established that the produced directories were byte-for-byte identical in both copies at that snapshot, so findings made on the unofficial copy applied to the produced code. Some commits in the unofficial copy also carried valid GitHub web-flow signatures, which authenticated its history, up to those commits, as it had existed on GitHub.

The limits were stated just as carefully. The match covered one snapshot, not the history of those directories. And the signatures authenticated the unofficial copy, not the production.

9 Checking a loose file against a repository

Someone hands you a single file and says it came from the codebase. Hash it, then ask the repository where that blob appears:

$ git hash-object ../loose/util.py
4af79c158719bdf44e8c6296c08019724f549d69
$ git log --all --oneline --find-object=4af79c1
ec7b6b5 Add tools directory
06ade68 Fix rounding in util.py
$ git hash-object ../loose/util-crlf.py
c967958f88e71e7c8fc4d542d51fb85e013ec70d
$ git log --all --oneline --find-object=c967958f88e71e7c8fc4d542d51fb85e013ec70d
(no output)

--find-object lists the commits that added or removed that blob at some path. Here those are the commit that introduced the fixed util.py and the commit that copied it into tools.

The second file is the same code saved with Windows line endings. One byte per line differs, so it is a different blob and the search finds nothing. A miss therefore does not prove the content was never in the repository. Line endings (core.autocrlf), a trailing newline, the text encoding or an editor’s reformatting are each enough to cause one. After a miss, normalize the file and try again, or fall back to comparing text.

Why this matters forensically

An exact match is conclusive and takes seconds. A non-match tells you only that the bytes differ. The reason still has to be found.

10 Renames, moves and copies

Git does not record renames, moves or copies. A commit holds a snapshot, and when you ask for a diff, Git guesses: if a file disappears from one path and the same or similar content appears at another, Git reports a rename.

$ git diff --name-status 06ade68 7058063
R100  docs/guide.md  docs/handbook.md
$ git diff --name-status --no-renames 06ade68 7058063
D  docs/guide.md
A  docs/handbook.md
$ git show --name-status --format= --find-copies-harder ec7b6b5
A  tools/run.sh
C100  src/util.py  tools/util.py

The same two snapshots read as “renamed” or as “deleted and added”, depending on a flag. R100 and C100 mean 100% similar, which is to say the blob hashes are equal. Below 100%, Git compares content against a similarity threshold (50% by default; -M90% raises it to 90%). Copies are found only if you ask (-C, --find-copies-harder). git log --follow uses the same guesswork to trace one file back through renames.

Why this matters forensically

“This file was moved from there”, “copied from there” and “rewritten from scratch” are inferences, not facts stored in the repository. Exact-hash matches are solid. For anything less, report the options and thresholds you used, because different settings can tell a different story.

11 Timestamps in depth

Each commit carries two dates. The author date is when the change was first written. The committer date is when this particular commit object was created. They start out equal and drift apart when a commit is rebased, cherry-picked or amended, because the author date is carried over and the committer date is reset.

$ git log --date=iso-strict --format='%h  %ad  %cd  %an'
a30b4b9  2024-03-15T10:00:00+00:00  2024-03-15T10:00:00+00:00  Ada Example
410cc9f  2024-03-08T09:30:00+00:00  2024-03-08T09:30:00+00:00  Ada Example
3d516dd  2024-03-07T10:20:00+00:00  2024-03-08T09:05:00+00:00  Ada Example
909aece  2024-03-07T15:45:00+05:30  2024-03-07T15:45:00+05:30  Raj Sample
253a528  2024-03-06T16:20:00+05:30  2024-03-06T16:20:00+05:30  Raj Sample
ec7b6b5  2024-03-06T16:05:00+05:30  2024-03-06T16:05:00+05:30  Raj Sample
7058063  2024-03-05T11:15:00+05:30  2024-03-05T11:15:00+05:30  Raj Sample
06ade68  2024-03-04T14:30:00+00:00  2024-03-04T14:30:00+00:00  Ada Example
727ea5c  2024-03-04T09:00:00+00:00  2024-03-04T09:00:00+00:00  Ada Example

Commit 3d516dd was authored on the 7th and committed on the 8th, which is what a rebase before merging looks like. The timezone offsets (+00:00, +05:30) come from each machine’s settings. They are a weak hint about where someone was working, and trivially changed.

Signals that deserve a closer look, none conclusive alone:

  • a committer date earlier than a parent’s;
  • many commits with identical or tightly bunched committer dates, which suggests a bulk rewrite;
  • author and committer dates far apart;
  • offsets that do not fit the supposed author.

What actually constrains time comes from outside the commit: signatures made with a key that existed or was valid only in a certain period, server-side records such as GitHub push events and pull-request timelines, CI logs, and any dated document that quotes a hash.

Why this matters forensically

Treat commit dates as statements by the author. They are useful for building a timeline and open to challenge. Tie the points that matter to something the author did not control.

12 Recovering deleted or unreachable material

Deleting a file in a commit removes it from later snapshots. Earlier commits still contain it. Even discarding a commit removes only the reference to it: the objects stay in the repository until garbage collection prunes them, usually weeks or months later.

In the demo, a commit containing a notes file was made and then immediately thrown away with git reset --hard:

$ git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs
unreachable tree d45d0e8966d149712f2207907df5bfebbedef231
unreachable blob dac272dee92e73d1be1516ff5e0adb1f37bb9e4d
unreachable commit 5d670a1b19e61696903517b3cfd630d5cbb1579b
unreachable tree f01054a6a2d802670f9d7748e1dc3a7d2d79ea74
$ git reflog -2
a30b4b9 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
5d670a1 HEAD@{1}: commit: WIP debug notes
$ git cat-file -p dac272d
db password: hunter2  (remove before committing!)
$ git -C ../fresh cat-file -t dac272d
fatal: Not a valid object name dac272d

No branch contains that file, yet the blob is still there and readable. The reflog, a local diary of where each branch has pointed, also remembers the discarded commit. Other places to look are git stash list, git notes, and refs outside refs/heads, which git for-each-ref lists (a mirror of a GitHub repository can include refs/pull/*).

The last command shows the catch: a fresh clone of the same repository does not have the object. What survives depends on how the copy was made.

How it was copied What you get
Raw copy of the .git directory Everything: unreachable objects, reflogs, stashes, config, hooks
git clone Objects reachable from branches and tags; no reflogs or stashes. (A clone from a local path can carry unreachable objects too)
Shallow clone (--depth) Recent commits only; earlier history is cut off
git bundle Only the refs and range its creator chose
Export and re-import, or filtering New hashes throughout (section 6)

Why this matters forensically

Ask how a repository was collected before drawing conclusions from what is absent. When you are the one requesting it, a forensic copy of the whole .git directory preserves far more than a clone does.

13 Brief notes

Submodules. A tree entry with mode 160000 holds the hash of a commit in a different repository. The parent repository pins exactly which version was used, but the code itself is not there. You need the other repository too.

Git LFS. Large files handled by LFS are replaced in the repository by small text pointers. Each pointer holds a SHA-256 of the real content, which is stored on a separate server. The blob hash covers the pointer, so matching tree hashes prove matching pointers. Verify the real files against the SHA-256 inside each pointer.

SHA-256 repositories. Git can create repositories that use SHA-256 throughout. Hashes are 64 characters, and the same content has unrelated hashes in the two formats, so compare like with like. Everything else in this primer applies unchanged.

14 Safe handling of evidence repositories

A repository is not inert data. Its configuration can make ordinary Git commands run programs, and some everyday commands rewrite or delete what is stored.

Before you run anything

  • Work on a copy. Hash the original first, for example a checksum of an archive of the whole directory, for chain of custody.
  • Read .git/config and .git/hooks/ in a text viewer. Settings such as core.fsmonitor, core.pager, core.sshCommand, gpg.program, diff.external and aliases can make routine commands execute arbitrary programs.
  • Prefer read-only commands: cat-file, ls-tree, rev-parse, rev-list, log, diff, fsck. Avoid checkout, pull, gc, repack and prune on evidence. gc can destroy unreachable objects.
  • Set GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0 so that commands like status do not write to the repository.
  • Record what you did: the Git version (git --version), the exact commands, and their output.

Cheat sheet

Open the printable one-page version (PDF)

Core ideas

  1. A blob is just bytes. Same bytes, same hash, anywhere.
  2. Names and permissions live in trees, not in files.
  3. Same tree hash: identical directory, all the way down.
  4. Same commit hash: identical snapshot and identical history.
  5. A valid signature vouches for its commit and every ancestor.
  6. Hashes prove identity. They do not prove time or authorship.
  7. Rewriting changes commit hashes. Untouched directories keep their tree hashes.
  8. Git infers renames and copies. It does not record them.
  9. Deleted rarely means gone, but it depends on how the copy was made.

Reading the commands

Angle brackets mark a value you supply. Type the value, not the brackets.

Notation Meaning
<commit> Any name for a commit: a full or shortened hash (a30b4b9), a branch (main), a tag (v1.0), or HEAD, the commit checked out now
<path> A file or directory, written from the top of the repository: src or src/util.py. <commit>:<path> names what was at that path in that commit
^{tree} Typed exactly as shown, braces included. After a commit or tag it means “the root tree this points to”, as in v1.0^{tree}. In Windows shells, put the whole name in double quotes
<obj>, <blob>, <a>, <b> The hash of an object, or any other name for it. <a> and <b> can be two commits or two trees

Inspect objects

Command What it tells you
git cat-file -t <obj> (also -s, -p) Type, size or content of any object
git ls-tree <commit> <path> A directory’s entries: mode, type, hash, name. -r lists every file
git rev-parse <commit>:<path> Hash of the file or directory at that path
git rev-parse <commit>^{tree} Hash of the commit’s root tree
git hash-object <file> Blob hash of any file on disk

Walk history

Command What it tells you
git rev-list --all Every reachable commit hash
git rev-list --first-parent --reverse <branch> The main line, oldest first
git rev-list --max-parents=0 --all Root commits (more than one is worth a look)
git log --date=iso-strict --format='%H %ad %cd %an' Author date and committer date side by side
git log --follow -- <file> One file’s history through inferred renames
git log --all --find-object=<blob> Commits that added or removed a blob

Compare

Command What it tells you
git diff --stat <a> <b> Files that differ between two commits or trees
git diff --name-status -M -C <a> <b> The same, with inferred renames and copies and their similarity
git diff --name-status --no-renames <a> <b> The same, with inference turned off

Signatures

Command What it tells you
git log --show-signature Signature check for each commit in the log
git verify-commit <commit>, git verify-tag <tag> Check one signature

Recovery

Command What it tells you
git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs Objects that no branch or tag reaches
git reflog Where HEAD has pointed (local copies only)
git for-each-ref Every ref, including ones outside branches and tags
git count-objects -v Loose and packed object counts
git bundle list-heads <file> The refs inside a bundle

Before you start: work on a copy, read .git/config and the hooks, and set GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0.
